title: A Review of Lattice Attacks Applied to Two Types of RSA Variants
abstract: In recent years, various RSA variants based on diverse algebraic structures have been proposed with the aim of enhancing its security. In this paper, we focus on type-A and type-B variants, which generalize RSA-type constructions over the ring of Gaussian integers modulo $N = pq$ and constructions based on the cubic Pell equation, respectively. First, we present a lattice-based method for finding, in polynomial time, solutions to the equation $xH(y)+cz\equiv 0 \bmod \beta$, where $H(y)$ is a monic polynomial, thereby generalizing previously established bounds. We then apply this method to factor the modulus in both type-A and type-B cryptosystems under multiple attack scenarios, such as partial key information attacks. Therefore, we provide certain bounds for the secret exponent under which these cryptosystems can be compromised.

      Abstract. In recent years, various RSA variants based on diverse alge-
      braic structures have been proposed with the aim of enhancing its secu-
      rity. In this paper, we focus on type-A and type-B variants, which gener-
      alize RSA-type constructions over the ring of Gaussian integers modulo
      N = pq and constructions based on the cubic Pell equation, respectively.
      First, we present a lattice-based method for finding, in polynomial time,
      solutions to the equation xH(y) + cz ≡ 0 mod β, where H(y) is a monic
      polynomial, thereby generalizing previously established bounds. We then
      apply this method to factor the modulus in both type-A and type-B
      cryptosystems under multiple attack scenarios, such as partial key in-
      formation attacks. Therefore, we provide certain bounds for the secret
      exponent under which these cryptosystems can be compromised.

1   Introduction

Background. The RSA cryptosystem, introduced by Rivest, Shamir, and Adle-
man in [31], remains a cornerstone of modern public-key cryptography and one of
the most ubiquitously deployed encryption schemes. In its standard formulation,
RSA operates in the multiplicative group ZN , where N = pq is the product of
two large primes. Encryption of a message m ∈ ZN is defined by c ≡ me mod N ,
where the public exponent e satisfies gcd(e, φ(N )) = 1 and φ(N ) = (p−1)(q−1).
Decryption is given by m ≡ cd mod N , with d ≡ e−1 mod φ(N ). The public key
is (N, e), whereas the factorization (p, q) and the secret exponent d remain con-
fidential. Throughout this work, we restrict attention to balanced primes, i.e.,
q < p < 2q, ensuring that p and q have equal bit-length.
    One of the fundamental problems of cryptanalytic research is the recovery
of the secret exponent d from the public key (N, e). Wiener’s seminal attack
[37] demonstrates that if d < N 0.25 /3, then d can be efficiently recovered from
the continued fraction expansion of e/N , thereby yielding a factorization of N .
Boneh and Durfee [3] substantially strengthened this result, showing that d <

RSA over Gaussian Integers. Elkamchouchi, Elshenawy, and Shaban introduced
in [12] an RSA analogue defined over the ring of Gaussian integers modulo
N . Instead of working with integers, their proposal uses elements of the form
a + bi, with a, b ∈ ZN and i2 = −1. The corresponding multiplicative group
ZN [i] has order ϕ(N ) = (p2 − 1)(q 2 − 1), and the public and secret exponents
satisfy gcd(e, ϕ(N )) = 1 and d ≡ e−1 mod ϕ(N ), respectively. Encryption and
decryption are defined exactly as in classical RSA, with all arithmetic performed
in ZN [i].
    Despite initial claims of enhanced security, Bunder et al. [4] demonstrated
a Wiener-type attack based on continued fractions. Subsequent refinements us-
ing lattice-based techniques [26, 38] extended this attack regime to d < N 0.585 .
Further cryptanalytic developments and refinements are discussed in [10, 32].

RSA based on the Cubic Pell Equation. Murru and Saettone introduced an
RSA-like cryptosystem in [23] based on a structured group formed by equiva-
lence classes of polynomials over GF (p3 ) × GF (q 3 ), where GF denotes a Galois
field. In contrast to classical RSA, the public exponent e is chosen to satisfy
gcd(e, ψ(N )) = 1, where ψ(N ) = (p2 + p + 1)(q 2 + q + 1). The corresponding
secret exponent is defined by d ≡ e−1 mod ψ(N ). Encryption and decryption
are carried out analogously to standard RSA, with all operations performed in
this specialized group rather than in ZN .
    As in the case of RSA over Gaussian integers, the authors initially claimed
that their construction was immune to classical RSA-like cryptanalytic attacks.
This claim was subsequently refuted in [24, 34], where it was shown that a
Wiener-type attack remains effective in this setting. Building on the Boneh–Durfee
methodology, Nitaj et al. [24] strengthened this attack, establishing the bound
d < N 0.5694 . Further refinements by Zheng, Kunihiro, and Yao [39] yielded the
sharper bound d < N 0.585 . Additional analysis and related developments are
discussed in [10, 32].

Generalizing via Galois Fields. The rings Zp and Zp [i] can be naturally iden-
tified with GF (p) and GF (p2 ), respectively, where GF denotes a Galois field.
Consequently, classical RSA may be viewed as operating over GF (p) × GF (q),
while the Gaussian variant corresponds to GF (p2 ) × GF (q 2 ). This algebraic
viewpoint led Cotan and Teşeleanu [10] to introduce a unified family of RSA-
like cryptosystems defined over GF (pn ) × GF (q n ) for n ≥ 1, with group order
φn (N ) = (pn − 1)(q n − 1). Encryption and decryption are direct generaliza-
tions of the cases n = 1 and n = 2. A similar endeavor was taken in [9] where
the authors extend the Murru-Saettone construction to equivalence classes of
polynomials over GF (pn ) × GF (q n ) for n > 1.

    The introduction of these two generic families—hereafter referred to as type-
A (RSA and its Gaussian variant) and type-B (Murru–Saettone)—was moti-
vated by the question of whether Wiener-type cryptanalysis extends to these
settings. Since then, a substantial body of cryptanalytic attacks has been devel-
oped against both families (e.g. [1, 11, 27, 35, 36]).

Our Contributions. Our first contribution is a lattice-based method for solving
equations of the form xH(y) + cz ≡ 0 mod β, where H(y) is a monic polynomial.
This result generalizes several existing methods [1, 18, 28, 29].
    This method is subsequently applied to the factorization of the modulus for
both cryptographic families (type-A and type-B) under multiple attack scenarios.
Specifically, we first consider the standard setting in which the adversary has
access only to the public key. We then analyze scenarios in which the adversary
additionally possesses either an approximation of p, knowledge that the prime
difference |p − q| is small, or partial information on the least significant bits of
d. All resulting bounds are compared with previously published cryptanalytic
results.

Structure of the Paper. We provide preliminary results in Section 2. In Section 3,
we show how to solve equations of the form xH(y) + cz ≡ 0 mod β, where
H(y) is a monic polynomial. We apply our result to different attack scenarios in
Section 4. Final remarks are given in Section 5.

5     Conclusions
In this paper, we presented a lattice-based technique for solving, in polynomial
time, modular equations of the form xH(y) + cz ≡ 0 (mod β) under certain
conditions. We then applied this approach to factor the module N = pq of
type-A and type-B cryptosystems. The resulting bounds were compared with
previously known results, demonstrating a significant improvement.
